newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan markets on alert for signs of policy change.
newsitem.headline: Japan markets on alert for signs of policy change.

text.p: With the U.S. and Japanese elections over, financial markets are looking for any clues that Tokyo's currency and monetary policies are ripe for change.
Analysts say Japanese policy makers -- worried that what goes down sharply could go up just as steeply -- have already signalled that further yen falls would be unwelcome.

But they also agree Japan's central bank is unlikely to boost its rock-bottom interest rates any time soon, given a sluggish recovery and concern about the more fragile elements of the nation's financial system.

"We are in no situation for the Bank of Japan (BOJ) to raise interest rates," said Masaru Takagi, chief economist at Fuji Research Institute. "There is not yet any evidence that this is a strong recovery, there are no inflation worries and there are still various problems in the financial sector."
Japanese government bond (JGB) futures prices slid sharply on Friday as a three-day correction to record highs hit on Wednesday continued.
JGB prices nosedived in early trade on a vague, unconfirmed rumour that a foreign news agency had carried an article suggesting a possible credit tightening.
JGB cash and futures were battered on Thursday after senior Finance Ministry official Eisuke Sakakibara said he believed Japan's economy was stronger than the market thought.
"Sakakibara said that the economy wasn't so bad, and maybe that rang a bell," one foreign economist said.

Economists said that authorities had probably been concerned that the bond rally had gone too far, but were unlikely to alter soon the hyper-easy credit stance adopted in September 1995 to ensure Japan's economy did not falter.
"Monetary policy is still on hold," said Peter Morgan, senior economist at James Capel Pacific.
"The economy is showing signs of recovery but my impression is that the BOJ is still worried about the effect of fiscal tightening and a consumption tax rise," he added.

A rise in Japan's three-percent consumption tax to five percent is planned from next April. Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's new government must meanwhile decide whether to draft a stimulative extra budget for 1996/97, a move some in his Liberal Democratic Party favour but which Finance Ministry officials oppose because of Japan's big budget deficit.

Talking up the yen a bit would also help the central bank to keep interest rates low, Morgan said. The yen slid to within a hair's breadth of 115 to the dollar last week, its lowest level in 42 months. "If they can jawbone the yen successfully, they don't have to worry about imported inflation," he said.
A weak yen raises import prices, which could in theory cause domestic prices to rise as well.

Financial markets were jolted on Thursday morning when a Japanese financial daily reported that Sakakibara had said the dollar's recovery from its sharp slide to a record low of 79.75 yen in April last year was about over.

Economists said Japan's authorities feared the steep and rapid yen drop could turn into an equally sharp surge. "The BOJ is worried that if the yen gets too weak, it could at some point move too strongly in the other direction," Morgan said.
A strong yen hurts the economy by dampening exports, making them more expensive abroad.

U.S. financial authorities, meanwhile, have been silent on exchange rates since U.S. President Bill Clinton's election, but many analysts believe both Washington and Tokyo could live happily with a dollar rate of above 100 yen but below 115.
